title: A grocery run, then breakfast by the water.
summary: A Saturday Hannaford stop during our off-season trip to Wells, Maine: Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and breakfast at a waterside picnic table.
search: Hannaford · Our off-season Wells tripA grocery run, then breakfast by the water.Oakhurst eggnog cold brew, our own plates and glasses, and a waterside picnic table. A simple Saturday breakfast idea from our Maine getaway, with a grocery stop James was very happy to make.October 18, 2026 · From the family notebook The makings of breakfast on our Wells trip, before we found our table by the water. On our trip to Wells, a quick Saturday morning stop at Hannaford became breakfast at a picnic table by the water. We had brought our own glasses and plates, so our grocery-store breakfast got a proper little table setting. I’ve loved Hannaford for years. I lived in Vermont for a long time, and it is one of those familiar places I’m always pleased to see when we’re away. I was hoping for my favorite butter rum muffins. They were sold out, which was a small disappointment, but we found plenty else to enjoy. We picked up assorted muffins, chocolate-frosted donuts, cold brew and Oakhurst eggnog. The eggnog added a Maine connection of its own: Oakhurst is a longtime Portland dairy. At our waterside table, we mixed eggnog into the cold brew and made our own eggnog coffee drinks. James had his eggnog on its own. It’s never off-season for eggnog. James had a good morning in the aisles, too. James loves grocery shopping. He was enjoying himself so much that other shoppers commented, and we proudly shared that he is often the grocery-store trip leader in his classroom. Shopping is one of his favorite things to do, and it was lovely to have a chance to tell people about that part of his school day. Then it was breakfast by the water: muffins, donuts, our little cold-brew experiment and time to sit together. We enjoyed it so much that we forgot to take a waterfront photo. The butter rum muffins can stay on the list for next time. Original editorial illustration, inspired by breakfast during our off-season Wells trip. A small idea to borrowBring the table setting. title: A date at the Gardner.
summary: A date at Boston’s Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, with our own photograph, practical caregiver planning, admission savings and museum accessibility notes.
search: The journal / Family & caregivers Boston, Massachusetts · Time for two A date at the Gardner. A beautiful place, a little time together, and a photograph of just the two of us. There is room for this part of family life, too. October 16, 2026 · From our family album Just the two of us at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. There is a place in our family album for just the two of us. Here we are at the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum, tucked beside a stone column, with that extraordinary courtyard behind us. A little Boston date, worth keeping. So much of family life happens in conversation about what needs doing next. The calendar, the ride, the groceries, the things that need remembering. I like having a photograph that holds something else: us, together, somewhere beautiful. The Gardner makes a lovely setting for that sort of outing. The courtyard gives you something to pause over before you have made a single decision about which room to see. Its plant displays change through the seasons; the museum’s own courtyard guide is a good place to see what might be there on a future visit. A museum date can be wonderfully modest. Choose a few rooms. Point out a detail you like. Ask which painting your partner would take home if such things were permitted. Leave enough time to enjoy being there without making the entire collection an assignment. Time together belongs in the family calendar. Make the date small enough to happen. For parents and caregivers, getting out together can take real arranging. Reliable help, money and a workable window of time all matter. When those pieces are available, a short date deserves a place in the plan. An hour or two can be a perfectly good beginning. Before booking, agree who is covering care, the return time, and how to reach you if needed. Put the essential information in one place; our caregiver handover guide can help. Build in the journey home so the last room does not become a race against the clock. Choose one main stop and let anything else be optional. The museum lists Café G for food and coffee; check its arrangements separately if you want to add it. Leaving after the museum is also a complete date. And if a museum visit is beyond this week’s budget or support arrangements, keep the idea of time together in a smaller form: a cup of tea after the house settles, a shared album, a few minutes talking about something you are both looking forward to. The people doing the caring belong in the picture, too. The practical details left inBefore your own Boston date. Tickets, timing & a less expensive dateThe museum is at 25 Evans Way, Boston. Advance timed tickets are recommended. Standard adult admission is currently $25; ages 17 and under enter free. It is closed Tuesdays. Check current hours and availability on the official visit page.Thursday evenings are free, 5–9 p.m. Registration opens Tuesday at 10 a.m., two days beforehand; walk-up admission is not guaranteed. Use the Free Thursday Nights page to book. Participating library passes offer $5 admission for up to four adults; you must reserve the pass and obtain timed tickets with its code. A free evening may be busy, so choose the timing that suits you. Mobility, seating & sensory considerationsThe museum reports elevators in both buildings and a Palace lift to bypass the two steps before its main elevator. Free loan wheelchairs, rollators and canes are limited and first come, first served. Historic rooms have varied flooring, narrow doorways and low lighting; some power chairs may not fit every doorway.Gallery benches are available, with fewer on the upper Palace floors. Public restrooms have accessible stalls. These are the museum’s published provisions; we have not tested each route or facility. For individual access questions, call 617-278-5156 and review the accessibility guide. Ask about a quieter visiting time if crowds or sound affect your plans. Arrival & parkingThe museum has no dedicated visitor parking lot. Its directions page lists nearby options, including discounted Simmons garage parking with museum validation. The access guide lists two designated accessible spaces and a ramped loading zone outside the museum, plus four accessible spaces on Tetlow Street. Allow time for the trip between parking and the entrance. Check the official directions and parking information before setting out. If you are planning a later visit with the familyThis photograph is from our couple’s outing. A family visit can have its own pace and plan. Preview the museum’s visitor guidelines, keep communication supports available, and ask staff about any essential items or accommodations before arriving. A short visit with a clear ending is a useful starting point. Visitor information checked October 16, 2026 against the museum’s pages linked above. Hours, offers and arrangements can change. title: A Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at Kohinoor
summary: A recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.
search: Kohinoor · Mashpee, MassachusettsA Little Heat on Cape Cod: Dinner at KohinoorA recommendation from a local artist led us to excellent Indian food in Mashpee—and a restaurant where our son was made to feel entirely welcome.By Michael, James’s dad · October 25, 2026James’s picture choice board ↓ James at Kohinoor in Mashpee. First things first: Kohinoor served us the best Indian food we’ve ever eaten. We love Indian food, we have eaten plenty of it, and we have opinions. This meal did nothing to make us less opinionated. We found the place through Laura DiMeo, the artist behind Perch Pottery in East Falmouth. We had reached out about visiting her studio, and she graciously welcomed our family for what became nearly two hours of conversation and a personal tour. Meeting an artist where she works is a pleasure in itself. Laura was also a delightful host. When the conversation turned to our fondness for Indian cuisine, she recommended Kohinoor Indian Restaurant & Bar in nearby Mashpee. We took her advice. Our order was entirely vegetarian: samosa chaat, aloo gobi, palak paneer, and garlic naan. We also happen to love heat. Serious heat. The kitchen had no difficulty accommodating us. The food The samosa chaat was an excellent introduction. Pieces of samosa mingled with chickpeas, onions, and tangy peppers; sweetness, bitterness, spice, and crunch kept turning up in different combinations. There was a lot going on, and every part of it seemed to belong there. Next came the aloo gobi. We ordered the potatoes and cauliflower very spicy, and the kitchen took us seriously. Very seriously. The impressive thing was how much flavor survived all that heat. Both vegetables were cooked perfectly and retained their individual textures. You could still taste the potatoes, the cauliflower, and the spices. The heat gave the whole thing considerable force without flattening everything beneath it. Making food hot is one thing. Making it this good at that level of heat takes some care. The palak paneer was equally convincing. Fresh-tasting spinach, soft paneer, and a rich, creamy sauce with enough heat to keep things interesting (yes, we ordered this one spicy, too). The creaminess and spice worked beautifully together. Nothing seemed to be compensating for anything else. And the garlic naan: fragrant, flavorful, crisp in places and gently chewy in others. An excellent companion to the curries, though it hardly needed their help. Not a single dish disappointed us. At the table with James Our teenage son, James, has significant support needs. He also likes going out with his family. We like finding places where all three of us can enjoy a meal without spending much of it explaining ourselves. My wife photographed the menu and used ChatGPT to make a choice board: eight options with pictures James could point to. He has his own opinions about dinner; the pictures give him another way to make them known. The choice board made for James from Kohinoor’s menu. The food pictures are AI-generated illustrations, not photographs of the restaurant’s dishes. Download James’s choice board (PNG)An independent picture resource based on the menu during our visit. Check current choices with your server, and keep familiar ways to say no, ask for help, or choose something else available.The staff were entirely comfortable with James. More than that, they seemed to get a kick out of him. Their warmth was easy and unforced, and they were attentive to the practical things. They brought his drinks in plastic cups with lids, a small but thoughtful detail that made the meal easier. When we requested a plastic spoon, one appeared almost immediately. None of this became an undertaking. The drinks arrived in cups that worked for him; we asked for a spoon and got one. That sort of straightforward attention goes a long way. As James’s dad, I am fairly alert to the difference between a restaurant tolerating our presence and actually enjoying having us there. Kohinoor gave us every reason to believe it was the latter. James was another guest, with a family and an appetite. No awkwardness required. The restaurant itself was immaculate: soft green walls, warm pendant lighting, floral accents, and comfortable booths. Even the small details—the patterned pots and white blooms—were worth a look. The service was impeccable throughout. A few of the small details: white blooms, patterned pots, and green walls. Worth the return trip I could recommend Kohinoor on the aloo gobi alone. The palak paneer, samosa chaat, and garlic naan make that recommendation considerably easier. So does a staff who made having dinner with our son feel as ordinary and enjoyable as it ought to. We went in hoping for a good Indian meal. We came out revising our list of favorites. Thank you, Laura, for the recommendation. And thank you, Kohinoor, for looking after us so well. We’ll be back. title: Words matter. So does context.
summary: How An AUsome Life approaches autism, disability, high-support needs and respectful representation.
search: Editorial standardWords matter. So does context.An AUsome Life uses clear, respectful language and avoids turning disability into either tragedy or inspiration content.Identity-first by defaultWe usually use “autistic person” rather than “person with autism,” while respecting an individual’s own preference when known.High-support / profoundWe use high-support language when it helps explain access needs. “Profound autism” may appear when discussing the specific high-support experience this publication covers; we do not present the term as universally preferred or as a hierarchy of human value.No pity framingSupport needs can be significant without making a disabled person a tragedy, lesson or campaign prop.Age-respectful alwaysTeenagers remain teenagers. We do not infantilize someone because their communication, learning or daily-living support needs are substantial.For brandsWe will not use cure/fixing language, staged distress, forced participation or intimate private details to make a story more emotional.
